title: Unit 1.2 Self-Assessment
subtitle: Relations and functions
intro: Twenty questions drawn from the unit 1.2 slides, either stated there directly or a short step of reasoning away. Work through them, then submit to see your score alongside the justification for each answer.

questions.prompt: How do the slides define a relation?

options.text: A set of ordered pairs, that is, a subset of the Cartesian product of two sets
Any rule that assigns exactly one output to each input
A set of numbers listed in increasing order
The set of all values a formula can take

questions.explanation: A relation is just a set of ordered pairs carved out of A × B, with a domain and a range. Assigning exactly one output to each input is the extra condition that makes a relation a function, which the slides introduce separately.

questions.prompt: Using the definitions of the basic types of relations, select every correct statement.

options.text: Reflexive means every element is related to itself
Symmetric means that if x is related to y, then y is related to x
Transitive means that if x is related to y and y to z, then x is related to z
Reflexive means no element is related to itself

questions.explanation: The three properties are stated on the slide in exactly these terms. Together they are what an equivalence relation has to satisfy.

questions.prompt: Which combination of properties defines an equivalence relation?

options.text: Reflexive, symmetric and transitive
Reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive
Symmetric and transitive only
Reflexive and symmetric only

questions.explanation: The slide defines an equivalence relation as reflexive, symmetric and transitive. Reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive is the order relation, listed beside it as the structure behind hierarchies.

questions.prompt: In the toy example, S is 'has the same major as', A is 'is at least as advanced as', and F is 'is a friend of', with friendships Jordan–Bob and Bob–Carol. Select every correct statement.

options.text: S is an equivalence relation, and it partitions the students into groups by major
A is an order relation, and it ranks the students
F fails transitivity, because Jordan is a friend of Bob and Bob of Carol while Jordan and Carol are not friends
F is an equivalence relation, because friendship is symmetric

questions.explanation: Symmetry alone is not enough. F is symmetric but fails both reflexivity, since nobody is listed as their own friend, and transitivity, so it is neither an equivalence nor an order relation.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes a function from a relation in general?

options.text: Each element of the domain is associated with exactly one element of the range
Each element of the range comes from exactly one element of the domain
The domain and the range have the same number of elements
The relation can be written as a formula

questions.explanation: The condition is on the domain side: one output per input. The second option is the one-to-one condition, which runs the other way, on the range side. It is a separate property rather than a stronger version of this one: in y² = 5x every y comes from exactly one x, yet it is still not a function.

questions.prompt: For f : A → B, what do the slides call the set of values actually reached by running every x in A through f?

options.text: The range, or image
The codomain
The domain
The Cartesian product A × B

questions.explanation: A is the domain and B the codomain, but B is only where the outputs are allowed to live. The range is the part of B that actually gets hit, and it can be smaller.

questions.prompt: A function may be many-to-one, but it may never be one-to-many.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: This is the rule the slides state directly. Several inputs sharing an output is fine: y = x² sends both 2 and −2 to 4. One input with several outputs is not, which is exactly why y² = 5x fails to be a function. One-to-many means one input paired with two different values in the same output set; a vector-valued function such as f : ℝ → ℝ² still returns a single element of ℝ², so it is not a counterexample.

questions.slide: Introduction of Functions (many-to-one vs one-to-many) · Relation that is not a function
questions.prompt: Why does y² = 5x fail to be a function of x?

options.text: For each x > 0 there are two values of y, namely +√(5x) and −√(5x)
Two different values of x can share the same y
Its graph is a parabola rather than a line
It cannot be written using elementary operations

questions.explanation: A function may not be one-to-many, and this relation assigns two y values to every positive x. Two inputs sharing an output is the many-to-one case, which is allowed, and plenty of parabolas, such as y = x², are perfectly good functions.

questions.prompt: For a linear function f(x) = b₀ + b₁x, how do the slides say b₁ should be read?

options.text: A one-unit increase in x changes f(x) by b₁, no matter where you start
A one-unit increase in x multiplies f(x) by b₁
b₁ is the value of f when x = 0
b₁ is the average of f over its domain

questions.explanation: The slope is the rate of change Δy/Δx, and for a linear function it is the same everywhere. That constancy is what makes the function linear. The value at x = 0 is the intercept b₀.

questions.slide: Why Slope Is the Point: A Regression
questions.prompt: In Y = β₀ + β₁X₁ + β₂X₂ + ε, with X₁ affective polarization and X₂ internal efficacy, what does β₁ represent?

options.text: The change in expected participation for a one-point widening of the thermometer gap, holding efficacy fixed
The expected participation of someone with no polarization and no efficacy
Everything the two predictors fail to account for
The share of participation explained by polarization

questions.explanation: β₁ is a slope, so it is a rate of change in Y per unit of X₁, with the other predictor held fixed. The second option describes the intercept β₀ and the third describes the error term ε.

questions.slide: Dimensions (f : ℝ² → ℝ¹, f(x, y) = 2x + y)
questions.prompt: What does f : ℝ² → ℝ¹ describe?

options.text: A function taking two real inputs and returning a single real number
A function taking one real input and returning two real numbers
A relation between two sets of real numbers that need not be a function
A function whose graph is a curve in the plane

questions.explanation: The slides' example is f(x, y) = 2x + y: each ordered pair (x, y) is assigned one number. The second option reverses the arrow, describing f : ℝ¹ → ℝ², which is a different and perfectly legitimate kind of function, just not the one written here.

questions.prompt: With f(x) = 2x and g(x) = x³, what is (g ∘ f)(x)?

options.text: 8x³
2x³
6x³
x³ + 2x

questions.explanation: g ∘ f means apply f first, then g: g(f(x)) = (2x)³ = 8x³. Applying them the other way round would give f(g(x)) = 2x³, which is the second option and a different function.

questions.prompt: The slides give f(x) = 3x + 2. What is f⁻¹(x)?
questions.explanation: Solve y = 3x + 2 for x: x = (y − 2)/3. The defining property is f⁻¹(f(x)) = x, so the inverse undoes the function. It is not the reciprocal, which is what the third option gives.

questions.prompt: The slides factor x³ − 5x² + 2x + 8 as (x + 1)(x − 2)(x − 4). What are the roots?

options.text: x = −1, 2 and 4
x = 5, 2 and 8

questions.explanation: A root is where the curve crosses the x-axis, so f(x) = 0. A product is zero when one factor is, and x + 1 = 0 gives x = −1 while x − 2 = 0 gives x = +2: each root is the value that zeroes its factor, so the signs flip.

questions.prompt: Applying the quadratic formula to x² + 3x − 4 = 0 gives which roots?

options.text: x = 1 and x = −4
x = −1 and x = 4
x = 2 and x = −2
There are no real roots

questions.explanation: With a = 1, b = 3, c = −4 the discriminant is 9 + 16 = 25, so x = (−3 ± 5)/2, giving 1 and −4. As a check, the factorisation is (x − 1)(x + 4).

questions.prompt: The slides state y = logₐ(x) ⇔ aʸ = x. What does this say about the two functions?

options.text: The logarithm is the inverse of the exponential with the same base
The logarithm is the reciprocal of the exponential
They are equal whenever a > 1
The logarithm is the exponential reflected across the x-axis

questions.explanation: Reading the equivalence in both directions is exactly the inverse relationship: the log undoes the exponential. Graphically this is a reflection across y = x, not the x-axis.

questions.prompt: Using the properties of exponents on the slide, and taking the base a > 0, select every correct statement.

options.text: aˣ · aʸ = aˣ⁺ʸ
(aˣ)ʸ = aˣʸ
a⁰ = 1
aˣ · aʸ = aˣʸ

questions.explanation: Multiplying powers adds the exponents; raising a power to a power multiplies them. The last option confuses the two rules. The slide states these without qualification, but they need a > 0 to hold for arbitrary real exponents: ((−1)²)^(1/2) is 1 while (−1)¹ is −1, and 0⁰ is undefined.

questions.prompt: Using the logarithm rules, log(x⁹y⁵ / z³) expands to:

options.text: 9 log(x) + 5 log(y) − 3 log(z)
9 log(x) · 5 log(y) / 3 log(z)
log(9x) + log(5y) − log(3z)
(9 log x + 5 log y) / 3 log z

questions.explanation: A product becomes a sum, a quotient becomes a difference, and an exponent comes down as a coefficient. The rules turn multiplication into addition, so the operations drop one level rather than being preserved.

questions.prompt: How do the slides define a monotonic function?

options.text: One that is either entirely non-increasing or entirely non-decreasing
One that is strictly increasing everywhere
One that has an inverse
One whose graph is a straight line

questions.explanation: Monotonic covers both directions and allows flat stretches, since non-decreasing rather than strictly increasing is enough. The slides note f(x) = 2x + 3, and log(x) on (0, ∞), as the strictly increasing cases.

questions.slide: Monotonic Functions · Monotonic Functions (cont'd): Why This Matters
questions.prompt: The slides state that if g is strictly increasing then arg max f(x) = arg max g(f(x)), and that log is strictly increasing. What follows for maximising a positive function f?

options.text: The x that maximises f also maximises log f(x), so either can be optimised
log f(x) attains its maximum at a different x, so the two problems are unrelated
The maximum value of log f(x) equals the maximum value of f(x)
Taking logs turns the maximisation into a minimisation

questions.explanation: A strictly increasing transformation preserves order, so it moves the height of the maximum but not its location. That is why the log-likelihood is maximised instead of the likelihood: it turns a product into a sum without moving the argmax. The maximum value does change, since log f(x*) is not f(x*).
